editorial_contributions.text: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a numbering \(f: V\to\{1,\dots,|V|\}\), the additive bandwidth of \(f\) is defined as \(B^+_f(G)=\max \{|f(u)+f(v)-(p+1)|: (u,v)\in E \}\), where \(p\) is some number. The additive bandwidth of \(G\) is the minimum of \(B^+_f(G)\) over all numberings \(f\). The authors relate the additive bandwidth with various graph invariants, such as the number of vertices, edges, independence number, chromatic number and minimal degree. They obtain lower and upper bounds for the sum of the additive bandwidth of \(G\) and its complement. Another key result is a lower bound for the sum of the additive bandwidth of \(G\) and the usual bandwidth of the complement of \(G\). These results show existence of graphs for which both the bandwidth and the additive bandwidth of both the graph and its complement are large.

editorial_contributions.text:
There are certain problems with the classical analogy between number fields and function fields. For example, the product of affine lines is the plane, but the product of \(\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) with itself is again \(\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\), and not a surface, because \(\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) is the terminal object in the category of schemes. Hence, results which are proved using algebraic geometry when working on the function field side, cannot be easily transported to the number field side, because the necessary algebraic geometry does not exist there.

The idea of the article under review is to forget the addition in a ring but remember multiplication of matrices. Using this insight the author constructs a category \(\mathbb{F}\), `the field with one element', which in a sense lies `below' \(\text{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\). He introduces the notion of an \(\mathbb{F}\)-ring and an \(\mathbb{F}\)-scheme and in particular proves that there is a fully faithful functor from commutative rings to \(\mathbb{F}\)-rings. One of several advantages of this language is that an arithmetical surface does exist, thus solving the above mentioned problem.

editorial_contributions.text: A \({\mathbb Q}\)-homology plane is a smooth algebraic complex surface \(X\) such that all the homology groups \(H_i(X;{\mathbb Q})\) with rational coefficients and \(i>0\) are trivial. Such a surface is always affine and rational. In this article, the authors study \({\mathbb Q}\)-homology planes on which there exists a non-trivlal action of the additive group \(({\mathbb C},+)\). The Makar-Limanov invariant of an affine variety \(X\) is the intersection of the kernels of all the locally nilpotent derivations on the ring of polynomial functions on \(X\). The main result of this paper is to show that any \({\mathbb Q}\)-homology plane \(X\) with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant is the quotient of the hypersurface in \({\mathbb C}^3\) defined by the equation of the form \(xy=z^m-1\) by a suitable action of \({\mathbb Z}/m{\mathbb Z}\), where \(m\) is the order of \(H_1(X;{\mathbb Z})\).

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: Robin Thomas asked whether for every proper minor-closed class \(\mathcal{G}\), there exists a polynomial-time algorithm approximating the chromatic number of graphs from \(\mathcal{G}\) up to a constant additive error independent on the class \(\mathcal{G}\). We show this is not the case: unless \(\mathrm{P}= \mathrm{NP}\), for every integer \(k\ge 1\), there is no polynomial-time algorithm to color a \(K_{4k+1}\)-minor-free graph \(G\) using at most \(\chi(G)+k-1\) colors. More generally, for every \(k\ge 1\) and \(1\le\beta\le 4/3\), there is no polynomial-time algorithm to color a \(K_{4k+1}\)-minor-free graph \(G\) using less than beta \(\chi(G)+(4-3\beta)k\) colors. As far as we know, this is the first non-trivial non-approximability result regarding the chromatic number in proper minor-closed classes.\par We also give somewhat weaker non-approximability bound for \(K_{4k+1}\)-minor-free graphs with no cliques of size 4. On the positive side, we present an additive approximation algorithm whose error depends on the apex number of the forbidden minor, and an algorithm with additive error 6 under the additional assumption that the graph has no 4-cycles.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1392.68012].

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The central problem discussed in this paper is that of deciding the recurrence or transience of 'random walk' on a regular grid in the plane, for example, the equilateral triangular grid, or the hexagonal grid. Such a process is a Markov chain, but the traditional Markovian methods of calculating n-step transition probabilities or absorbing probabilities only work in the simplest examples. Some, though not all, of such processes are true random walks to which the results of \textit{K. L. Chung} and \textit{W. H. J. Fuchs} [Mem. Am. Math. Soc. 6 (1951; Zbl 0042.375)] apply; in general, however, such a process contains an embedded random walk whose recurrence or transience (to be decided by Chung-Fuchs) determines that of the original process. A general result on the recurrence of an additive functional (with values in an Abelian group) of a Markov chain is proved.

editorial_contributions.text:
A vector \(X=(x_ 1,...,x_ n)\) (where \(x_ 1<x_ 2<...<x_ n\) are relatively prime integers) is called a basis of additive permutations (an A-basis) if there exists a permutation \(Y=(y_ 1,...,y_ n)\) of X such that the vector sum \(X+Y=(x_ 1+y_ 1,...,x_ n+y_ n)\) is again a permutation of X. Every integer interval (-k, \(-k+1,...,k)\) is known to be an A-basis. Each additive permutation of an integer interval can be represented by a collection of points in a regular hexagon in the plane. 


The following transformations of such a hexagon yield again an additive permutation: 1. Rotation about the centre of the hexagon by an integer multiple of 60 degree. 2. Reflection in a straight line joining the centre of the hexagon and a vertex. 3. Reflection in a straight line joining the centre of the hexagon, and the centre of a side. The purpose of the paper is to study the invariants of these transformations.

editorial_contributions.text:
Some forty years ago, in connection with the (Eichler) cohomology of automorphic forms, \textit{M. Eichler} [Acta Arith. 11, 169--180 (1965; Zbl 0148.32503)] introduced (what later came to be called) the ``generalized Poincaré (in particular, Eistenstein) series''. Following this lead, Lehner and, somewhat later, the reviewer made use of Eichler's generalized Poincaré series in proving versions of the Eichler cohomology theorem. In these earlier applications the series in question are holomorphic in \(H\), the upper half-plane.

 More recently, Goldfeld and his school initiated a natural new direction in the study of such series, considering a nonholomorhpic (real-analytic in \(H\)) version analogous to the nonanalytic Poincaré series introduced by Hecke in 1921. This path-breaking work of Hecke shifted the focus from the \(z\) variable (\(z\) in \(H\)), with respect to which Hecke's series behave like modular forms on a subgroup \(\Gamma\) of \(\text{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})\), to the new \(s\) variable, with \(s\) in a right half-plane. These series are holomorphic in \(s\) for \(\text{Re\,}s\) sufficiently large; Hecke succeeded in continuing them analytically into an open half-plane containing \(s= 0\) and, consequently, in constructing nontrivial modular forms of weights 1 and 2 on \(\Gamma\).

 In the paper under review the authors continue the study of nonanalytic generalized Poincaré series and apply their results to the estimation of character sums on finitely generated Fuchsian groups \(\Gamma\) of the first kind. The characters in question are mappings from \(\Gamma\) into \(\mathbb{C}\). The presence of these (weight 0) characters distinguish the generalized Poincaré series (holomorphic in \(z\) or not) from the usual Poincaré series, as they replace the multiplicative characters (i.e., weight 0 multiplier systems) that occur in the latter. This replacement entails a loss of group invariance, with respect to \(\Gamma\), which is, however, supplanted by a more complicated, three-term analogue for the generalized series. The application to estimating character sums is a striking development, which appears to have the potential for extension to sums over \(\Gamma\) of nonzero-weight additive cocycles on \(\Gamma\). The estimation requires extensive analysis of the generalized Poincaré series, including especially analytic continuation in the variable \(s\). The authors emphasize the relatively difficult case of noncuspidal additive characters on \(\Gamma\). (Cuspidal characters are those that vanish on all parabolic generators of \(\Gamma\)).

editorial_contributions.text: Compact Riemannian manifolds have discrete spectrum, and spectral gaps are important properties and have many applications. For noncompact complete hyperbolic manifolds, the spectrum of the Laplace operator is not discrete anymore, and the essential spectrum is given by a continuous spectrum, and this reflected in resonances, or singularities of the resolvent kernel in the complex plane. In this case, spectral gaps for the essential spectrum refer to the existence of regions which contain the upper halfplane and admits only finitely many singular points. In this paper, the authors ``obtain an essential spectral gap for \(n\)-dimensional convex co-compact hyperbolic manifolds with the dimension \(\delta\) of the limit set close to \(\frac{n-1}{2}\). The size of the gap is expressed using the additive energy of stereographic projections of the limit set. This additive energy can in turn be estimated in terms of the constants in Ahlfors-David regularity of the limit set.'' The proofs ``use new microlocal methods, in particular a notion of a fractal uncertainty principle.''

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We study the coverage properties of Bayesian confidence intervals for smooth component functions of generalized additive models (GAMs) represented using any penalized regression spline approach. The intervals are the usual generalization of the intervals first proposed by Wahba and Silverman in 1983 and 1985, respectively, to the GAM component context. We present simulation evidence showing that these intervals have close to nominal `across-the-function' frequentist coverage probabilities, except when the truth is close to a straight line/plane function. We extend the argument introduced by \textit{D. Nychka} [J. Am. Stat. Assoc. 83, 1134--1143 (1988)] for univariate smoothing splines to explain these results. The theoretical argument suggests that close to nominal coverage probabilities can be achieved, provided that heavy oversmoothing is avoided, so that the bias is not too large a proportion of the sampling variability. The theoretical results allow us to derive alternative intervals from a purely frequentist point of view, and to explain the impact that the neglect of smoothing parameter variability has on confidence interval performance. They also suggest switching the target of inference for component-wise intervals away from smooth components in the space of the GAM identifiability constraints.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The problem of minimizing the sensitivity of the output or input of a plant under a feedback control with respect to external additive disturbances is considered. The mathematical model assumed for the plant is a rectangular matrix of transfer functions which can arise from both lumped-parameter and distributed-parameter systems (including time delays). The feedback controller is assumed to guarantee the closed-loop stability. It is shown that an arbitrary small sensitivity function on a compact set of complex frequencies can be obtained by a suitable choice of feedback transfer function, provided no zero of the plant transfer function is in this set. Additionally, the sensitivity function can be designed to be bounded on an unbounded region containing the imaginary axis, if there are no zeros of the plant in the right half-plane and a certain hypothesis holds. Multiplicative delays are not excluded. If there are zeros in the right half-plane the latter design is not realizable, since minimizing the sensitivity on a bounded interval implies its increasing without bounds on the remaining part of the imaginary axis (an appropriate inequality is derived).

editorial_contributions.text:
The authors consider the stochastic differential equations 
\[
 dx =(\alpha x-\beta y-(ax-by)(x^2+y^2))dt+\sigma dW_t^1, 
\]
 
\[
 dy =(\alpha y+\beta x-(bx+ay)(x^2+y^2))dt+\sigma dW_t^2, 
\]
 where \(W_t^1\) and \(W_t^2\) are independent one-dimensional Brownian motions. The aim of the paper is to provide an analysis of the stability regimes of this system in terms of its parameters. The two crucial parameters are \(b\) (the shear strength) and \(\alpha\) (which controls the Hopf bifurcation that occurs when \(\sigma=0\)). For fixed \(a,\beta,\sigma\) the \((b,\alpha)\)-plane is partitioned into three regions with different stability behaviour. In region I (\(\alpha\leq 0\) and \(b\) small) the system has a random attractor with uniform synchronisation of solutions. In region II there is nonuniform synchronisation (i.e., finite-time instabilities occur but the asymptotic behaviour is exponentially stable for almost all trajectories. In region III the largest Lyapunov exponent is positive, there is no synchronisation and the system has a random strange attractor. A number of results are proven, and the authors conjecture that irrespective of the value of \(\alpha\), for strong enough shear the system is in region III.

editorial_contributions.text: Chentsov type representation theorem is proved for stochastically continuous, linearly additive, infinitely divisible random field without Gaussian component, where a random field \(X=\{X(t),\;t\in R^ d\}\) is called linearly additive if the stochastic process \(\xi\) defined by \(\xi(\lambda)=X(a+\lambda b)\), \(\lambda\in R\), has independent increments for every pair \((a,b)\), \(a,b\in R^ d\). In passing it is shown that there exists a natural one-to-one correspondence between stochastically continuous, linearly additive Poisson random fields on \(R^ d\) and locally finite, bundleless measures on the space of all \((d-1)\)- hyperplanes in \(R^ d\). The latter result is closely related to Ambartzumian's theorem on the representation of linearly additive pseudo- metrics in the plane.

editorial_contributions.text:
Numerical analysis for integral equations of type identity plus compact operators is well developed and almost completed. But most of interesting boundary integral equations arising in applications, first of all in mathematical physics, are not of this type and include integral (integro-differential) equations with singular kernels of Cauchy and Calderon-Zygmound type on curves and surfaces with singularities. Numerical analysis for equations of such type is far from being complete. Their numerical treatment is based on a substantially refined theory of approximation methods based on the observation that the stability problem is an invertibility problem in a certain Banach or C*-algebra (first noted by \textit{A. V. Kozak} in [Sov. Math., Dokl. 14, 1580--1583 (1973); translation from Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 212, 1287--1289 (1973; Zbl 0306.46058)]). As a rule, this algebra is complicated and one has to use local principles and representation theory to establish the invertibility results. 

The present book treats numerical methods for one dimensional boundary singular integral equations, arising in mathematical physics (mostly in 2-dimensional mechanics). The book is addressed to a wide audience and might be useful for both pure mathematicians working in theoretical fields of numerical analysis and engineers wishing to have practically realizable concepts for computations.

What is characteristic for this book and other books written by the members of the research group headed by B. Silbermann, that the obtained results, including the stability of approximation methods, are formulated as criteria (necessary and sufficient conditions). This is rather impressive and is achieved by involving very modern tools of functional analysis and operator theory, including localization methods in Banach algebra and para-algebras, developed by the authors. These achievements fully compensate a ``pure academic'' style of the exposition, which is sometimes too difficult to follow for engineers and colleagues from applied mathematics.

The authors start with a careful development and exposition of tools from complex and real algebras, operator theory, Fredholm theory of one dimensional singular integral and Mellin convolution operators, different local principle (of Gohberg-Krupnik, of Allan and in para-algebras) and many others. Simultaneously they refine approximation methods: Galerkin's, spline collocation, \(\varepsilon\)-collocation, spline qualocation etc. (see Chapter 1).

In Chapter 2 the authors study polynomial Galerkin and collocation methods, apply them to singular integro-differential equations with complex conjugation. Further they develop \(\varepsilon\)-collocation, spline Galerkin, quadrature, polynomial qualocation and spline qualocation methods to apply them in the forthcoming chapters.

Chapter 3 is devoted to Riemann-Hilbert and Riemann-Hilbert-Poincaré problems, including the case of piecewise-continuous coefficients.

In Chapter 4 stability of approximation methods are investigated for singular integral equations with complex conjugation in \(L_2(\Gamma)\) spaces. The local principle is applied and local representatives of singular integral operators for the quadrature method, for the \(\varepsilon\)-collocation and qualocation methods are detected. Fredholm properties and the invertibility of local representatives are carefully investigated to accomplish the approximation method, prove the convergence and stability. 

Similar results in subsequent sections are obtained for the spaces \(L_{2,\omega}(\Gamma)\) with piecewise-smooth curve \(\Gamma\) and exponential weight \(\omega(t)=\prod_{j=1}^n|t-\gamma_j|^{\rho_j}\), \(\gamma_j\in\Gamma\). The obtained results are refined and developed further for double layer potential operators and Mellin operators with complex conjugation.

Chapter 5 is devoted to the boundary value problem for the biharmonic equation \(\Delta^2u(x,y)=0\) in a 2-dimensional domain \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^2\). Although the problem is thoroughly studied [see e.g. \textit{P. Grisvard}, Elliptic problems in nonsmooth domains. Monographs and Studies in Mathematics, 24. Pitman Advanced Publishing Program. (Boston-London-Melbourne): Pitman Publishing Inc. (1985; Zbl 0695.35060)], the authors suggest yet another approach, based on the theory of functions of a complex variable. They use the representation of a biharmonic function by two analytic functions, common in the plane elasticity theory. The problem is reduced, as in the plane elasticity, to a Muskhelishvili singular integral equation with Cauchy kernel and complex conjugation. Some known results on the Fredholm properties and solvability of Muskhelishvili equations in \(L_p\) spaces with exponential weights are exposed. As next the authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions which ensure the convergence and stability of Galerkin approximation, of \(\varepsilon\)-collocation and qualocation methods for smooth contours. Results for Galerkin approximation of Muskhelishvili equations on piecewise-smooth contours accomplish the chapter. 

In the concluding Chapter 6 the authors demonstrate the theoretical results on concrete Muskhelishvili equations and biharmonic problems. They obtain numerical results for the collocation and Galerkin methods and expose corresponding tables and graphs.

Each chapter in the book is endowed with rather detailed comments and references.

u\) denotes the free additive convolution for \(\mu, 
u \in {\mathcal D}_c(k)\), where \( oxplus\) is a binary operation on the space of probability distributions on \({\mathbb R}\), reflecting the additive operation for free random variables in a non-commutative probability space.

One of the peculiar features in the theory [cf.\ 	extit{P.\ Biane}, Math.\ Z.\ 227, No.\,1, 143--174 (1998; Zbl 0902.60060)] is the fact that the Cauchy transform \(G_{\mu  oxplus 
u}\) of the distribution \(\mu  oxplus 
u\) is subordinated to the Cauchy transforms of \(\mu\) and of \(

\[
 G_{\mu  oxplus 
u}(z) = G_{
u} ( \omega(z)), \quad  orall z \in {\mathbb C}^+, 	ag{1} 
\]
 and the subordination function \(\omega\) can be identified as the reciprocal Cauchy transform of a uniquely determined probability distribution \(\sigma\) on \({\mathbb R}\). If \(\sigma\) is written temporarily as \(\mu  oxdot 
u\), then \(\sigma =\) \(\mu  oxdot 
u\) is nothing but \(s\)-free additive convolution of \(\mu\) and \(
u\) in 	extit{R.\ Lenczewski} [J.\ Funct.\ Anal.\ 246, No.\,2, 330--365 (2007; Zbl 1129.46055)]. The author just calls it the subordination distribution of \(\mu  oxplus 
u\) with respect to \(
u\), because \(s\)-freeness is only marginally addressed in the present paper.

The goal of the paper is to introduce and study the analogue for \(\mu  oxdot 
u\) in a multi-variable framework, where \(\mu, 
u\) become joint distributions of \(k\)-tuples of selfadjoint elements in a \(C^*\)-probability space. The author derives an explicit formula for the moments of the subordination distribution, which leads to an operator model on the full Fock space. This gives a recipe which starts from the data stored in the \(R\)-transforms \(R_{\mu}\) and \(R_{
u}\), and uses creation and annihilation operators on the full Fock space over \({\mathbb C}^{2k}\) in order to produce a \(k\)-tuple of operators with the subordination distribution. It can also be shown that, for every distribution \(
u \in {\mathcal D}_c(k)\) being the joint distribution of a standard semicircular system (= a free family of \(k\) centered semicircular elements of variance 1), the subordination distribution \(\gamma  oxdot 
u\) of \(\gamma  oxplus 
u\) with respect to \(
u\) is realized as \({\mathbb B}( \Phi(
u))\), where \({\mathbb B}\) is the Boolean Bercovici-Pata bijection [cf.\ 	extit{H.\,Bercovici} and 	extit{V.\,Pata}, Ann.\ Math.\ (2) 149, No.\,3, 1023--1060 (1999; Zbl 0945.46046)], \(\Phi :\) \({\mathcal D}_{alg}(k) 	o {\mathcal D}_{alg}(k)\) is a certain transformation which carries \({\mathcal D}_c(k)\) into itself, satisfying

\[

u  oxplus \gamma^{ oxplus t} ) = {\mathbb B}_t( \Phi(

u \in {\mathcal D}_{alg}(k), \quad  orall t \geq 0, 	ag{2} 
\]
 
\({\mathcal D}_{alg}(k)\) is the set of all purely algebraic distributions, and \(\{ {\mathbb B}_t \mid t \geq 0 \}\) is a family of bijective transformations of \({\mathcal D}_{alg}(k)\) defined by 

\[
 {\mathbb B}_t(\mu) = ( \mu^{ oxplus (1 + t)})^{ \uplus 1 / (1 + t)}, \quad  orall t \geq 0, \quad  orall \mu \in {\mathcal D}_{alg}(k), 	ag{3} 
\]

u \in {\mathcal D}_c(k)\) and for every \(p \geq 1\), the subordination distribution of \(
u^{ oxplus p}\) with respect to \(

The main tools used in this paper are combinatorial properties of \(R\)-transforms for joint distributions and a related operator model, with operators acting on the full Fock space. It is interesting to note that multi-variable subordination turns out to have nice relations to a process of evolution towards \( oxplus\)-infinite divisibility on \({\mathcal D}_c(k)\), and also has a connection with free Brownian motion. editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Necessary and sufficient conditions for Stochastic Stability (SS) and Mean Square Stability (MSS) of continuous-time linear systems subject to Markovian jumps in the parameters and additive disturbances are established. We consider two scenarios regarding the additive disturbances: one in which the system is driven by a Wiener process, and one characterized by functions in \(L_2^m(\Omega,{\mathcal F}, \mathbb P)\), which is the usual scenario for the \(H_{\infty}\) approach. The Markov process is assumed to take values in an infinite countable set \(\mathcal{S}\). It is shown that SS is equivalent to the spectrum of an augmented matrix lying in the open left half plane, to the existence of a solution for a certain Lyapunov equation, and implies (is equivalent for \(\mathcal{S}\) finite) asymptotic wide sense stationarity. It is also shown that SS is equivalent to the state \(x(t)\) belonging to \(L_2^n(\Omega,{\mathcal F}, \mathbb P)\) whenever the disturbances are in \(L_2^m(\Omega,{\mathcal F}, \mathbb P)\). For the case in which \(\mathcal{S}\) is finite, SS and MSS are equivalent, and the Lyapunov equation can be written down in two equivalent forms with each one providing an easier-to-check sufficient condition.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper is concerned with incidence problems involving translates of a convex curve. Let \(C\) be a fixed convex curve. Let \(P\) be a set of \(n\) points in \(\mathbb R^2\) and let \(L\) be a family of \(n\) translates of \(C\). It follows from (a variant of) the Szemerédi-Trotter Theorem that the number of incidences between \(P\) and \(L\) is at most \(O(n^{4/3})\). The question of possibly getting better bounds is a major open problem in combinatorial geometry. In particular, if \(C\) is a unit circle, this incidence problem corresponds precisely with the Erdős unit distance problem, and any improvement to the upper bound \(O(n^{4/3})\) for the number of pairs of points from a given set which are a distance \(1\) apart would be big news.

One cannot hope to improve on the upper bound \(O(n^{4/3})\) in general, since it is known that there exist convex curves which really can have a number of incidences of this order, although these convex curves are known to be somewhat exceptional (see [\textit{N. Alon} et al., ``Unit and distinct distances in typical norms'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:2302.09058}]).

This paper provides an inverse theorem for when many incidence do occur. The inverse theorem gives information about the way that the translates are structured (as opposed to some classification of the possible convex curves). Roughly speaking, the main result states that, if such a configuration really does give \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) incidences, then the set of translates of \(C\), denoted by \(T \subset \mathbb R^2\), has a large subset which is efficiently contained in a low degree generalised arithmetic progression. An application to a variant of the unit distances problem is also given.

title.title: Concurrent shape optimization of the part and scanning path for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing

editorial_contributions.text:
A flag in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a figure consisting of a point \(P\in \mathbb{R}^3\), a line \(\gamma\) through \(P\) and a plane through \(\gamma\). If we consider the families of flags depending on a line \(\gamma\), we obtain families which are homeomorphic to the product \(\gamma\times E_1 (\gamma)\), where \(E_1 (\gamma)\) is the circle of length \(\pi\) of the (planar) directions orthogonal to \(\gamma\). The simplest sets of this type are the so called wedges which have the product form \(w= \nu\times \lambda\), where \(\nu\subset \gamma\) is an open interval and \(\lambda\subset E_1 (\gamma)\) is an open arc. In combinatorial integral geometry the idea of finitely additive functionals \(\Psi\) depending on a function \(F\) defined in the space of wedges arises from results on the measure in the space \(E\) of planes in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): in this context wedge functions depend on the measure defined in \(E\) and the corresponding functionals serve to calculate values of this measure on subsets of \(E\). 


In this paper, the authors tackle the following problem: given a wedge function, what are the conditions so that it determines a signed measure on \(E\)? 


The main result of the paper is a theorem that gives necessary and sufficient conditions which guarantee that a given functional \(\Psi\) generates a locally finite signed measure in \(E\). In particular, the author considers wedge functions generated by ``flag densities'', i.e. functions which are integrals on the wedge of continuous functions defined in the space of flags. Then, under an additional smoothness hypothesis, the conditions are formulated by using combinations of the values of \(F\) depending on a pyramid (pyramidal excess). More precisely, if this pyramidal excess has infinitesimal order greater than \(h^2\) (where \(h\) is the height of the pyramid) on sequences of flattening pyramids, then \(\Psi\) generates a signed measure in \(E\); moreover this measure is nonnegative if the pyramidal excess is nonnegative. 


The authors also present some analytical consequences of such conditions. They show by means of a ``first-order analysis'' that the flag densities have the form of a sinusoid and derive a differential equation for their parameters. They leave the complete solution of the problem (``second-order analysis'') to a successive paper.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Rotation number elementary theory for Birkhoff curves has been constructed. Geometrical (dynamical) and numerical properties for Birkhoff curves being more than two regions common boundary has been studied. Topological number invariants with respect to a dissipative dynamic system on the plane possessing the Birkhoff curve property have been discussed. Simple allocation algorithm of natural numbers has been applied, so that its Schnirelmann density is equal to the rotation number for a region. If the region boundary is a Birkhoff curve then the sequence contains an additive basis zero Schnirelmann density. The basis contains an arbitrary long arithmetic progression. Rotation numbers for regions are defined to be different additive bases zero Schnirelmann density.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(a\), \(b\) and \(k\) be fixed integers with \(k \geq 3\). The authors' result is a strong quantitative form of the proposition that almost all of the integers \(n\) represented by the binary form \(ax^k-by^k\) are so representable in an essentially unique way (i.e., in a way not differing in other than the sign or order of \(x\), \(y\)).


Let \(\mu(X)\) denote the exceptional set of the number of these \(n\) with \(|n|\leq X\) that have multiple representations, so that the trivial estimate would read \(\mu(X) \ll X^{2/k}\). The authors' result is \(\mu(X) \ll X^{c/k+\epsilon}\), for a certain explicitly given \(c=c(k)<2\) with \(c \sim {3 \over 2}\) as \(k \to \infty\). Thus they can estimate the total number of \(n\) with \(|n|\leq X\) represented by the form, by an expression incorporating an error term \(O( X^{c/k})\).


In the case when \(a = \pm b\) there are results already in the literature. Using a sieve method and Deligne's estimates for exponential sums \textit{C. Hooley} obtained a result with \(c \sim {5 \over 3}\) when the degree \(k\) is odd [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc., III. Ser. 43, 73-109 (1981; Zbl 0463.10035)], which he has more recently extended to even \(k\) in the case \(a=b\) [J. Reine Angew. Math. 475, 55-75 (1996; Zbl 0848.11041)]. Actually these results have \(c = {5 \over 3}\) if \(k=3\), or if \(a=b\). Furthermore when \(k=3\) \textit{D. R. Heath-Brown} [Acta Arith. 79, No. 1, 17-30 (1997; Zbl 0863.11021)] has improved the result to \(c={4 \over 3}\), by a development of an elementary approach due to Wooley. Hooley has also obtained weaker results for more-or-less arbitrary forms of degree three, and for a wide class of forms of degree four.


The present authors' result is the first to apply when \(|a|\neq |b|\) and when \(k \geq 5\). They employ a ``slicing'' approach previously used by \textit{C. M. Skinner} and \textit{T. D. Wooley} in the case \(a=b\) [J. Reine Angew. Math. 462, 57-68 (1995; Zbl 0820.11059)]. In this approach, the problem is reduced to one concerning the number of points on a carefully selected collection of plane curves, which are then attacked using a theorem of \textit{E. Bombieri} and \textit{J. Pila} [Duke Math. J. 59, No. 2, 337-357 (1989; Zbl 0718.11048)].


This approach raises the possibly serious difficulty that these curves, of degree \(k\), have to be shown to be absolutely irreducible. One approach to this question is to try to show that they have no singular points. The authors' method depends on showing rather less, viz. that they have less than \(k-2\) singular points.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The additive dimension for a common boundary of the Wada basins bases (and Wada ocean) accessible points has been defined. One is constituted to be value being inverse to fractional density for the sequence (basis) zero Schnirelmann density and one characterizes only metric property of the boundary (Birkhoff curve). The additive dimension is similar to Hausdorff-Besicovitch dimension. All Wada basin and Wada ocean are quite metrically characterized to be only additive dimension of accessible points. It follows that additive dimension is invariant with respect to a plane diffeomorphism.

editorial_contributions.text:
The author introduces the notion of Markov field on the plane which is modified in the following way. Let \((E,{\mathcal E})\) be a measurable space, \(\Delta \in E\), \(E_\Delta =E \cup \{ \Delta\}\). Let \({\mathcal E}_\Delta\) be a \(\sigma\)-field on \(E_\Delta\) generated by \(\mathcal E\) and \(\{ \Delta\}.\) Let \(P^x\) be a family of probability measures on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\), where \(x \in E_\Delta\) and the \(\sigma\)-fields \(\{ {\mathcal F}_t\), \(t \in \mathbb{R}^2 \}\) satisfy the usual conditions. Let \(\theta_t: \Omega \to \Omega\) be a family of maps, \(t \in \mathbb{R}_+^2\), \(\theta_t = \theta_{t_1}^1 \ast \theta_{t_2}^2.\) Let \(x_t: \Omega \to E_\Delta\) be \({\mathcal F}_t\)-measurable random fields. editorial_contributions.text: A function \(u(z)\) is said to be differentially algebraic (DA) if it satisfies a non-trivial algebraic differential equation (ADE), that is, an equation of the form \(P(z,y(z),\dots, y^{(n)}(z))= 0\), where \(P\) is a polynomial with complex coefficients in its \(n+2\) variables. It is called respectively differentially real, differentially homogeneous, and differentially additive, if the respective function \(\bar u(\bar z)\), \(c(z)\), \(u(z)+ c\) (\(c\) is any complex constant) satisfies every ADE which is satisfied by \(u(z)\). The author proves the following statements: If \(f\) is DA and real on \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(g\) is any differentially real entire function, then the composition \(f\circ g\) is differentially real. If \(u\) is a non-constant DA entire function with no zeros on the complex plane, then \(u\) is differentially homogeneous. Suppose \(g\) is a DA entire function algebraically dependent over the differential field generated by \(g'\) and suppose further that the order of any minimal polynomial for \(g\) is \(n\). Then any minimal polynomial for \(e^ g\) is of order \(n+1\).

editorial_contributions.text:
The author offers novel proofs of the classical results that additive functions on reals, bounded from one side on an interval are linear, while the graph of a nonlinear additive function is everywhere dense in the real plane, and also similar results on vector spaces.


Fundamental is the following observation. Let \(f\) be (throughout this review) an additive function from the vector space \(E\) into the vector space \(F\). If \(E\) and \(F\) are real vector spaces, \(r\) a real number and \(x\) an element of \(E\) then \(f(rx)-rf(x) = f(\{r\}x)-\{r\}f(x)\), where \(\{r\}\) is the fractional part of \(r\). We denote by \(D(f;r)(x)\) the left hand side of this equality and by \(D(f;F)\) the subspace of \(F\) generated by \(D(f;r)(x)\). If \(E\) and \(F\) are topological vector spaces and the image of \(E\) under \(f\) is a subset of \(D(f;F)\) then the graph of the nonlinear \(f\) is dense in the cartesian product of \(E\) and of \(D(f;F)\). If \(f\) is continuous at a point of the topological vector space \(E\) then it is linear. If \(E\) and \(F\) are normed spaces and \(f\) bounded in a neighborhood of one point then it is linear and continuous.


Several examples are offered of ``small'' sets \(S\) of real numbers such that the graph of every nonlinear real additive function on \(S\) is dense on the cartesian product of \(S\) and of the set of real numbers.


\{Note: The remarkable proof by G. S. Young, quoted on p. 164, concerned additive functions bounded on a proper interval from both sides. However, the generalization to functions bounded from one side is easy\}.

editorial_contributions.text: An additive hereditary property of graphs is a class of simple graphs that is closed under unions, subgraphs and isomorphisms. Let \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\) be additive hereditary properties of graphs. The property \(\mathcal{Q}^{n}\) is defined as follows: A finite simple graph \(G\) belongs to \(\mathcal{Q}^{n}\) if and only if \(G\) has a vertex partition \(\{V_{1},\dots ,V_{n}\}\) such that for each \(i=1,\dots ,n\) the induced subgraph \(G[V_{i}]\) belongs to \(Q\). The generalized chromatic number \(\chi _{\mathcal{Q}}\left( \mathcal{P}\right) \) is the least integer \(n\) such that \(\mathcal{P\subseteq Q}^{n}.\) In this paper \(\chi _{\mathcal{Q}}\left( \mathcal{P}\right) \) is investigated for several well-known properties \(\mathcal{Q}\) and \(\mathcal{P}.\)

editorial_contributions.text:
The Grötzsch problem is a classical result of \textit{H. Grötzsch} [Berichte Leipzig 80; 367--376, 497--502 (1928; JFM 54.0378.01)] which says that the linear stretch map is the minimizer for the maximal distortion among the class of quasiconformal homeomorphisms between two rectangles which map the horizontal edges into the corresponding horizontal edges and requiring respectively the same condition on the vertical edges. Grötzsch established criteria to measure how to approximate conformality between two plane domains. The minimizer for the maximal distortion among the class of quasiconformal homeomorphisms is called an extremal quasiconformal map. How to find the extremal quasiconformal maps is a critical problem in the theory of quasiconformal maps.

In this paper, the authors search for extremal quasiconformal maps on a different measure space: the affine-additive group, which from the topological viewpoint is one of the eight 3-dimensional Thurston geometries. The authors first build a modulus method which relies on the minimal stretching property of the map for a given curve family foliating the domain of definition. Then, they define linear and radial stretch maps in the affine-additive group, and prove that they are minimizers of the mean quasiconformal distortion functional. They show that this designed method detects quasi-conformal maps between domains of the affine-additive group. The effect is that the authors obtain extremal stretch maps minimizing the mean distortion functional in the class of all quasiconformal mappings between two such domains.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(C\) be an affine plane curve. The author considers additive functions \(f: K \to K\) for which \(f(x)f(y) = 0\), whenever \((x, y) \in C\). He shows that if \(K = \mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\) this is the hyperbola with defining equation \(xy = 1\). Therefore there exist nonzero additive functions with this property.

After that, the author shows that there exists an additive function \(f: \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(x)f(\frac{1}{x}) = 0\) (when \(x \neq 0\)) which is not identically zero on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Furthermore, he also considers the general problem over finite fields. Let \(\mathbb{C}\) be an absolutely irreducible smooth curve and let \(f: \mathbb{F}_{p^k} \to \mathbb{F}_{p^k}\) be an additive function such that \(f(x)f(y) = 0\) whenever \((x, y)\in \mathbb{C}\).

Finally, by using the classical Hasse-Weil bound on the number of points of a smooth absolutely irreducible curve defined over a finite field, he is able to show that if the degree of the curve is small compared to the characteristic of the field, then \(f\) must be identically zero. The approach can be applied to higher-dimensional varieties as well.

editorial_contributions.text: The author provides some facts about \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\)-Maass forms. The Maass forms here considered are analogous to the classical Maass forms on the upper half plane. The author studies smooth functions \(F\) on \(\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb R)/(O(n,\mathbb R) \cdot \mathbb R^{\times})\) which are invariant under the action of \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\). These are eigenfunctions of the center of the universal enveloping algebra of \(\mathfrak{gl}(3,\mathbb R)\). The center of the universal enveloping algebra of \(\mathfrak{gl}(2,\mathbb R)\) is generated by the hyperbolic Laplacian. The function \(F\) satisfies a cuspidality condition. Similar to the classical Maass forms, \(F\) has a Fourier expansion and has an associated \(L\)-function. The Fourier coefficients of \(F\) are naturally indexed by two parameters. The author gives some identities and relations on additive twisted of Fourier coefficients of \(\mathrm{GL}(3)\)-Maass forms.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Let a group $G$ act linearly on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$. The group-additive diameter of a subspace $U \leq V$ is the least number of translates of $U$ whose sum is all of $V$. Counting dimensions, it is at least $\dim V / \dim U$. We show that when $G$ is compact and $V$ is irreducible, the diameter of every nonzero subspace is at most $\lceil (\dim V / \dim U) \ln \dim V \rceil$, so the trivial bound is correct up to a logarithmic factor. We measure the discrepancy by the covering complexity $\mathsf{C}(V)$, the largest ratio between the diameter of any subspace and its trivial lower bound, so that $1 \leq \mathsf{C}(V) \leq 2 + \ln \dim V$, and we determine where in this range various representations lie. Every irreducible representation of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf{C})$ has $\mathsf{C}(V) = 1$. The logarithm can be genuinely present along families of symmetric and exterior powers of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbf{C})$ with $n$ varying, and it is present for finite Heisenberg groups and $2$-transitive groups of small order such as $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbf{F}_p)$. The complexity is bounded above by a constant on the conjugation representations of $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbf{C})$ and on the representations $\operatorname{Sym}^k \mathbf{C}^3$ of $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbf{C})$. On the other hand, every fixed connected reductive group has a family of irreducible representations whose complexities tend to at least the dimension of the flag variety. Finally, for the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_3(\mathbf{C})$ acting on $\operatorname{Sym}^k \mathbf{C}^3$, the monomial diameter with respect to $\operatorname{Sym}^k X$ for a plane $X \leq \mathbf{C}^3$ is optimal, while the corresponding $\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbf{C})$ diameter is not.

editorial_contributions.text: In the paper in J. Comb. Theory, Ser. A 39, 42-51 (1985; Zbl 0624.28012) \textit{S. P. Gudder} and \textit{J. E. Zerbe} proved that for finitely valued functions the integral on quantum probability spaces (QPS) is additive. Their proof involved highly nontrivial combinatorial reasoning. By applying a new (essentially plane topological) method, we extend the additivity result to a broad class of functions. [Theorem 6: Let \((X,L,s)\) be a QPS and let f, g, \(f+g\) be bounded measurable functions on X. Let the ranges of f and g be nowhere dense sets in R and let the range of g be countable. Then \(\int (f+g)ds=\int f ds+\int g ds.]\) When specialized to finitely valued functions, we also provide a simpler proof of the original Gudder-Zerbe theorem.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let 
\[
 E_2(T) = \int_0^T|\zeta({\textstyle{1\over2}}+it)|^4\text{ d}t - TP_4(\log T) 
\]
 denote the error term in the asymptotic formula for the fourth power moment of the Riemann zeta-function \(\zeta(s)\), where \(P_4(y)\) is a polynomial of degree four in \(y\) with leading coefficient \(1/(2\pi^2)\). \textit{Y. Motohashi} [Ann. Sc. Norm. Super. Pisa, Cl. Sci., IV. Ser. 22, 299-313 (1995; Zbl 0831.11046)] recently introduced the function \(Z_2(s) = \int_1^\infty |\zeta({\textstyle{1\over2}}+ix)|^4x^{-s} \text{ d}x\), which is absolutely convergent for \(\text{Re }s> 1\). He has shown that \(Z_2(s)\) has meromorphic continuation over the whole complex plane. In the half-plane \(\text{Re }s > 0\) it has the following singularities: the pole \(s = 1\) of order five, simple poles at \(s = {1\over2} \pm i\kappa_j (\kappa_j =\sqrt{\lambda_j - {1\over4}})\) and poles at \(s = \rho/2\), where \(\rho\) denotes complex zeros of \(\zeta(s)\). Here as usual \( \{\lambda_j = \kappa_j^2 + {1\over4}\} \cup \{0\} \) is the discrete spectrum of the non-Euclidean Laplacian acting on \(SL(2,{\mathbb{Z}})\)-automorphic forms. By using properties of \(Z_2(s)\), Motohashi (op. cit.) showed that \(E_2(T) = \Omega_\pm(T^{1/2})\), and this result was put into a quantitative form by the reviewer [``On the Mellin transform and the Riemann zeta-function'', Proc. Conf. on analytic and elementary number theory, Vienna July 18-20, 1996, 112-127 (1996)]. Now the authors also use \(Z_2(s)\) to prove the following interesting result (and an analogue for the error term in the additive divisor problem): There exist constants \(c > 0\) and \(r_0 > 0\) such that for every \(0 < a < r_0\) we have, as \(T \to \infty\), 
\[
 \mu\{ 1 \leq x \leq T: E_2(x) > a\sqrt{x} \} = \Omega(T/\log^cT), \tag{1}
\]
 and an analogous result for \(E_2(x) < -a\sqrt{x}\), where \(\mu(\cdot)\) denotes Lebesgue measure. The basis of the proof is a Landau-type theorem for Mellin transforms, which is in fact a Tauberian-type result of independent interest. In the case of \(E_2(T)\) the proof of (1) relies on the bound \(\int_0^TE_2^2(t)\text{ d}t \ll T^2\log^CT\), proved by \textit{Y. Motohashi} and the reviewer [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. 69, 309-329 (1994; Zbl 0805.11060)]. The authors also prove that 
\[
\int_T^{2T}E_2^2(t)\text{ d}t = \Omega(T^2),
\]
 but it should be mentioned that the reviewer [``On the error term for the fourth moment of the Riemann zeta-function'', J. Lond. Math. Soc. (in press)] recently improved this to \(\int_0^{T}E_2^2(t)\text{ d}t \gg T^2\).

editorial_contributions.text: If \([m]= \{1,\dots, m\}\), \(m\) a positive integer, consider the three-dimensional box \(B= [p]\times [q]\times [r]\), with \(S\) a subset of \(B\). The idea of a reduction of a set is introduced and an equivalence relation is defined on \(B\). Two subsets of \(B\) are box equivalent if both can be reduced to a third set; every set in this class can be reduced to it. A set \(S\) in \(B\) is additive if and only if any reduction of \(S\) is additive. A special class of subsets called pyramids is introduced and it is pointed out that there is a one-to-one correspondence between these and plane partitions, already known to P. A. MacMahon.

editorial_contributions.text:
If $\mathcal{P}$ is a set of $N$ points in the plane, let $\Delta (\mathcal{P})$ denote the set of (squared) distances spanned by $\mathcal{P}$. \textit{P. Erdős} [Am. Math. Mon. 53, 248--250 (1946; Zbl 0060.34805)] conjectured that 

$$\vert \Delta (\mathcal{P})\vert =\Omega(N/\sqrt{\log N}).$$ 

\textit{P. Erdős} [Discrete Math. 60, 147--153 (1986; Zbl 0595.52013)] conjectured that each extremal configuration has a lattice-like structure. \textit{L. Guth and N. H. Katz} [Ann. Math. (2) 181, 155--190 (2015; Zbl 1310.52019)] proved that $\vert \Delta (\mathcal{P})\vert \gg N/\log N.$ 

In the paper under review the author proves that, for any finite set $A$ of real numbers, 

$$\vert A-A\vert \ll \vert \Delta(A\times A)\vert \vert A\vert ^{-1/8}.$$ 

Consequently, if $\mathcal{P} = A\times A$ determines few distances (near $c\vert A\vert ^2/\log \vert A\vert)$  then $$\vert A-A\vert \ll \vert A\vert ^{2-1/8}.$$

editorial_contributions.text: The Neumann problem for the Laplace equation in the exterior of a curve in the plane is considered. The author reformulates the problem as a boundary integral equation of the first kind with a symmetric kernel. Both the \(h\) and \(p\) versions of the Galerkin scheme are considered. The author proves that the condition number of the additive Schwarz operator is bounded by \(\mathcal O(1+\log ^2(H/\delta))\) for the \(h\) version, where \(H\) is the size of the coarse mesh and \(\delta\) is the size of the overlap, and is bounded independently of the mesh size and the polynomial order for the \(p\) version. Numerical results for the \(h\) version are presented.

editorial_contributions.text:
This paper presents the lecture notes from the course given at AGRA II, in Cusco/Peru. The area of additive combinatorics began in the context of studying the structure of sets of integers with respect to the operations of addition and multiplication. As an introduction, the author shows that many questions concerning the integers can also be formulated in abelian groups or finite fields.

We define the sumset as \(A+B = \{a+b : a \in A, b \in B\}\). It is easy to see that \(\max\{|A|,|B|\} \leq |A+B| \leq |A||B|\). Section 1 presents several bounds, such as:

-- the classical result stating that \(|A+A| \geq 2|A|-1\), with equality if and only if \(A\) is an arithmetic progression,

-- the Cauchy-Davenport Theorem, which states that \(|A+B| \geq \min\{p,|A|+|B|-1\}\) if \(A,B \subset \mathbb{Z}_p\),

-- Plünnecke's Inequality, which states that if \(A,B \subset G\) are finite and \(|A+B| \leq K|A|\), then \(|kB-mB| \leq K^{k+m}|A|\) for all positive integers \(k,m\),

-- the Freiman-Ruzsa Theorem, which states that if \(A \subset \mathbb{F}_p^n\) satisfies \(|A+A| \leq K|A|\), then \(A\) is contained in a subspace \(H \leq \mathbb{F}_p^n\) of cardinality at most \(K^2 p^{K^4}|A|\), along with a reformulation of this result and further developments in this direction (see Theorem 1.11, Conjecture 1.12, and Theorem 1.13).

In Section 2, incidence geometry and the sum-product phenomenon, the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem is presented. In the plane, given a set \(P\) of points and a finite set \(L\) of lines, how many incidences can there be between points in \(P\) and lines in \(L\)? Let \(I(P,L) = |\{(p,\ell) \in P \times L; p \in \ell\}|\). Clearly \(I(P,L) \leq |P||L|\). The Szemerédi-Trotter theorem asserts that \(I(P,L) \le 4|L|^{2/3}|P|^{2/3} + 4|P| + |L|\).

Later, in Subsection 2.2, the sum-product phenomenon over the real numbers is presented. The product-set \(A \cdot A = \{aa'; a,a' \in A\}\) has cardinality ranging between \(|A|\) and \(|A|^2\). Note that the cases of minimal cardinality differ greatly between the sumset and the product set. The sumset is minimized when \(A\) is an arithmetic progression, but in that case the product-set is very large. On the other hand, when \(A\) is a geometric progression, the product-set is minimized, but the sumset attains maximal cardinality. Thus, it is natural to ask whether both can be small simultaneously. Formally, the Erdős-Szemerédi Conjecture states that if \(A \subset \mathbb{R}\) is finite, then for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\max\{|A+A|, |A \cdot A|\} \gg |A|^{2-\varepsilon}\). It has been proven that \(|A+A|^2 |A \cdot A|^2 \gg |A|^5\), and then \(\max\{|A + A|, |A \cdot A|\} \gg |A|^{5/4}\). Subsection 2.3 discusses the same phenomenon over finite fields, which turns out to be somewhat more intricate than the case over \(\mathbb{R}\).

In Section 3, the author first discusses the polynomial method. The combinatorial \textit{Nullstellensatz} is presented, which states that if \(f \in \mathbb{F}_p[t_1,\dots,t_n]\) has degree \(d\) and a nonzero coefficient in \(t_1^{d_1}\dots t_n^{d_n}\) with \(d_1+\dots+d_n = d\), and if \(S_1,\dots,S_n \subset \mathbb{F}_p\) are such that \(|S_i| > d_i\) for every \(i\), then there exist \(x_1 \in S_1, \dots, x_n \in S_n\) such that \(f(x_1,\dots,x_n) \neq 0\). Subsequently, the Euclidean Kakeya problem is discussed. A Kakeya set in dimension \(n\) is a subset in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) that contains a unit line segment in every direction. The central question is whether it is possible to construct Kakeya sets that are ``small'' in a certain sense. Finally, in Subsection 3.3, the Kakeya problem is studied over finite fields.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(G\) be a subgroup of \(\operatorname{O}(n)\) and let \(H\) be a closed subgroup of \(G\cap \operatorname{O}(n-1)\), where \(\operatorname{O}(n-1)\subset \operatorname{O}(n)\) is the stabilizer of the first basis vector. In the following, \(\operatorname{Area}_{G/H}^G\) denotes the space of smooth flag area measures that are equivariant with respect to \(G\). These objects are translation invariant valuations that take values in the space of signed measures on \(G/H\) and that can be represented by certain smooth differential forms.

In their main result, the authors show that \(\operatorname{Area}_{G/H}^G\) is finite-dimensional if and only if \(G\) acts transitively on the unit sphere and that in this case there exist local additive kinematic formulas of the form \[\int_G \Phi_i(K+g L,\kappa\cap g \lambda) d g = \sum_{k,l=1}^N c_{k,l}^i \Phi_k(K,\kappa) \Phi_l(L,\lambda).\] Here, \(\{\Phi_1,\ldots,\Phi_N\}\) is a basis of \(\operatorname{Area}_{G/H}^G\), \(\kappa,\lambda\) are Borel subsets of \(G/H\) and \(K\) and \(L\) are convex bodies. Note that these formulas can be encoded by a cocommutative, coassociative coproduct.

For \(G\subset \operatorname{SO}(n)\) the elements of \(\operatorname{Area}_{G/\{1\}}^G\) are also called rotation measures and an explicit construction and classification of such measures is given. Furthermore, the authors give an algebraic description of the kinematic formulas for \(\operatorname{Area}_{G/H}^G\) when \(H\subset \operatorname{SO}(n-1)\) is a closed subgroup. In particular, an explicit description of this algebraic structure is given for the important case \(G=\operatorname{SO}(n)\), \(H=S(\operatorname{O}(p)\times \operatorname{O}(q))\), \(p+q=n-1\), in which \(G/H=\operatorname{Flag}_{1,p+1}\) is the incomplete flag manifold consisting of pairs \((v,E)\), where \(E\) is a \((p+1)\)-plane and \(v\in E\).

Note that the results of this paper generalize previous results by [\textit{T. Wannerer}, Adv. Math 263, 1--44 (2014; Zbl 1296.53150)] and [\textit{A. Bernig}, Geom. Dedicata 203, 85--110 (2019; Zbl 1432.53099)].

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The characteristic equation for a linear delay differential equation (DDE) has countably infinite roots on the complex plane. We deal with linear DDEs that are on the verge of instability, i.e. a pair of roots of the characteristic equation (eigenvalues) lie on the imaginary axis of the complex plane, and all other roots have negative real parts. We show that, when the system is perturbed by small noise, under an appropriate change of time scale, the law of the amplitude of projection onto the critical eigenspace is close to the law of a certain one-dimensional stochastic differential equation (SDE) without delay. Further, we show that the projection onto the stable eigenspace is small. These results allow us to give an approximate description of the delay-system using an SDE (without delay) of just one dimension. The proof is based on the martingale problem technique.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Let $\mathscr{B}(\mathscr{H})$ be the Banach algebra of all bounded linear operators on a complex space $\mathscr{H}$. It is proved that an additive surjective map $\Phi$ on $\mathscr{B}(\mathscr{H})$ preserves nonzero partial isometries of products of two operators in both directions if and only if there is a unitary operator or anti-unitary operator $\boldsymbol{U}$ on $\mathscr{H}$ such that $\Phi(\boldsymbol{X}) = \lambda \boldsymbol{UXU}^*$, for all $\boldsymbol{X} \in \mathscr{B}(\mathscr{H})$ for some constant $\lambda$ with $\lambda \in \mathbb{T}$, where $\mathbb{T}$ is the unit circle in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. Moreover, we characterize the additive surjective mappings preserving Jordan triple products of two operators.

Let \(k\) be a field, \(A\) a \(k\)-domain, \(A[T]\) the polynomial ring in one variable over \(A\), and \(\sigma :A\to A[T]\) a homomorphism of \(k\)-algebras. Then \(\sigma \) defines an action of the additive group \({\mathbf G}_a =\mathbf{Spec}\;k[T]\) on \(\mathbf{Spec} A\)

Due to \textit{R. Rentschler} [C. R. Acad. Sci., Paris, Sér. A 267, 384--387 (1968; Zbl 0165.05402)], \textit{M. Miyanishi} [Nagoya Math. J. 41, 97--100 (1971; Zbl 0191.19201)] and \textit{H. Kojima} [Colloq. Math. 137, No. 2, 215--220 (2014; Zbl 1315.14079)], the invariant ring for a \({\mathbf G}_a\)-action on the affine plane over an arbitrary field is generated by one coordinate.

This nice paper provide a new short and very elegant proof for this result using the automorphism theorem of \textit{H. W. E. Jung} [J. Reine Angew. Math. 184, 161--174 (1942; Zbl 0027.08503)] and \textit{W. van der Kulk} [Nieuw Arch. Wiskd., III. Ser. 1, 33--41 (1953; Zbl 0050.26002)].

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The influence of lattice structures on the propagation of elastic waves in these structures is analyzed. The statement of problem is formulated within the framework of linear elasticity under small strains. To solve this problem, the finite element method and the Fidesys CAE-system were used. Different variants of plane lattice structures are modeled: the classical lattice and the lattice with uniformly curved strips across the plane: elevator and star-shaped lattices. The relation between the structure of lattice structures and the propagation of perturbations in these structures is analyzed. The dependence of wave velocity in curved lattice structures on the frequency of the emitted waves is analyzed. An applied conceptual model of the device for measuring the frequency of waves is developed.

These preconditioners work in the same way as when they are used for the Galerkin boundary element method: the condition numbers of the preconditioned stiffness matrices grow at most logarithmically with the degree of freedom. Several numerical results are presented to support the theory.

editorial_contributions.text: An additive hereditary property of graphs is a class of simple graphs that is closed under unions, subgraphs and isomorphisms. Let \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(\mathcal{Q}\) be additive hereditary properties of graphs. The property \(\mathcal{Q}^{n}\) is defined as follows: A finite simple graph \(G\) belongs to \(\mathcal{Q}^{n}\) if and only if \(G\) has an edge-decomposition \(\left\{ E_{1},\dots ,E_{n}\right\} \) such that for each \(i=1,\dots ,n\) the induced subgraph \(G[E_{i}]\) belongs to \(Q\). The generalized edge-chromatic number \(\rho _{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime }\left( \mathcal{P}\right) \) is defined as the least integer \(n\) such that \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq n\mathcal{Q}\). In this paper \(\rho _{\mathcal{Q}}^{\prime }\left( \mathcal{P}\right) \) is investigated for specific well-known properties \(\mathcal{Q}\) and \(\mathcal{P}.\)

editorial_contributions.text: The authors give necessary conditions for a subgroup \(G\) of the abelian group \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to be either a straight line or the whole group itself. These conditions are (1) \(G\) is connected and contains a straight line segment, and (2) \(G\) contains a subset of the form \(\{(x,f(x))\}\) or \(\{(f(x),x)\}\) for some continuous, non-linear function \(f\colon(a,b)\to\mathbb{R}\). As a corollary they derive Yamabe's theorem (Any arcwise connected subgroup of a Lie group is a Lie group) for the plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Without exception the arguments they use are elementary, giving a nice proof of Yamabe's theorem for \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

editorial_contributions.text:
The aim of this paper is similar to the one of Ambartzumyan and Oganyan (see the preceding review) but it is devoted to functionals on planar bounded convex polygons. Given a functional \(\Psi\) defined on ``needles'' (oriented segments) and given a natural extension of \(\Psi\) to bounded convex polygons, if \(\Psi\) can be represented as an integral of a twice differentiable function defined on the flags (a flag being a pair \((P,h)\) with \(P\) a point and \(h\) an half-plane whose boundary contains \(P\)) then, under some additional conditions, \(\Psi\) determines a signed measure on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). 


The author also shows that the case of a functional \(\Psi\) defined on the ``corners'' (oriented angles) can be reduced to the needle case and it also treats the mixed case.
